messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Publisher
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Vulnerability: Being naked, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Vignette:
Omar was a 34-year-old Middle Eastern man who had built a steady life in publishing, commuting into the city, meeting authors, and spending long hours at a desk before heading home to his wife. Before the trauma, he described himself as confident in the ordinary routines of adulthood, someone who knew how to move through crowded streets and public spaces without much thought. That changed after a violent assault on his younger brother, a university student who had been returning home on a bus in the evening. Omar had not been there in person, but he had received the call while his brother was still alive, panicked and unable to speak clearly. In the days that followed, the family pieced together that the attack had happened in a confined public place, with strangers nearby, and that his brother had been stripped of any sense of control and left exposed and helpless. The details Omar learned afterward became lodged in his mind in a jagged, incomplete way. He could recall flashes of the bus interior, the sense of alarm in his brother’s voice, and the harsh sound of the emergency call, but the sequence never came together cleanly. He described the memory as arriving in disconnected pieces that did not fit, as if he had been handed fragments of a scene he could not fully assemble.

In the months after the assault, Omar found that the trauma returned to him not as a complete story but as something that replayed on its own. At unexpected moments he would feel as though the event were unfolding again, like a film that had started without his permission and kept running in his mind. When he tried to think about what had happened, he sometimes seemed to hear the same sounds that had been present that night, especially the voices and noises that had accompanied the frightening call and the frantic efforts to understand where his brother was and whether he would survive. These intrusions were vivid enough to pull him away from whatever he was doing, and they left him feeling shaken, disoriented, and unable to settle back into the present. At night, after the house had gone quiet, the replay was often more intrusive, and he found himself listening for echoes of the event in his own head.

Omar also began to move through the world as if danger could appear anywhere and at any time. He had come to study people’s faces and body language with unusual intensity, scanning for the slightest sign that someone might be a threat. In offices, on sidewalks, and in the lobby of his building, he found himself reading expressions rather than listening to conversations, noticing hands, shoulders, posture, and the way strangers carried themselves. He also became acutely aware of potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, his attention snagging on sharp tools in a conference room, heavy items in a train station, or anything that could be used to harm. Unfamiliar places felt especially difficult. As a publisher, Omar sometimes had to attend book events, dinners, or meetings in neighborhoods he did not know well, but he began to avoid going to unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger there. What had once been a normal part of his work now required careful calculation, and over time he turned down invitations and chose only the locations he knew best.

Certain bodily states brought the fear closer. Being naked, especially when exhausted, made him feel acutely exposed. He noticed this most at home after long workdays, when he was very tired or exhausted and was getting ready to shower or change clothes. In those moments he became more unsettled, as if fatigue lowered the guard he needed to keep himself and his family safe. He would sometimes hurry through simple routines, wanting to be covered again as quickly as possible. Public transport also became difficult. Because his brother had been attacked on a bus, riding buses now carried a heavy charge for Omar, and he avoided them whenever possible, even when they would have been the most practical option for commuting or reaching a part of the city. If he had no choice, he endured the ride with visible strain, watching the other passengers, the doors, and the movements around him, trying to stay oriented until he could get off.

By the time he sought help, Omar’s life had become smaller and more demanding. His wife had noticed how much energy it took him to get through an ordinary day, and how often he seemed preoccupied, tense, or absent. At work he remained functional but increasingly limited, choosing familiar routes, familiar locations, and familiar people whenever he could. He came to treatment because he was exhausted by the constant sense of being on alert and because the memories were no longer staying in the background where he wanted them. What frightened him most was that the image of his brother’s assault could still seize him so completely, and what he hoped for was not to forget his brother, but to be able to remember without feeling as though he were back on that bus, waiting for something terrible to happen again.
